title: When Scaffolding Breaks: Investigating Student Interaction with LLM-Based Writing Support in Real-Time K-12 EFL Classrooms
venue: Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI ’26)
extended_summary:
This paper examines how large language models (LLMs) function as real-time writing support in K-12 English as a Foreign Language (EFL) classrooms, focusing on whether step-by-step scaffolding actually helps students during in-class writing. The authors ask how students with different proficiency levels interact with an LLM, how those interaction patterns relate to learning and retention, and how introducing the tool changes classroom dynamics and teacher roles.

The intervention was WriteAid, a chat-based LLM writing assistant designed to provide scaffolded help rather than direct answers. It supported sentence construction, vocabulary and grammar explanations, and grammar revision through tabs, and was used during two classroom writing exercises over six weeks. The study was conducted in a public middle school in South Korea with 157 eighth-grade students; 133 consented for analysis. The researchers combined system-log analysis, qualitative coding of interaction data, a naturalistic observation study, and analysis of a delayed written assessment.

Findings showed that the LLM improved grammatical accuracy and helped students complete writing tasks, but its step-by-step support had mixed effects. Higher-proficiency students used the tool more efficiently and often for lower-level tasks such as vocabulary translation and validation, while lower-proficiency students more often relied on it for sentence and paragraph generation, became more dependent on the system, and sometimes felt demotivated or frustrated by the scaffolded interaction. The classroom observations also showed that the tool shifted teacher attention patterns, reduced some routine question handling, and created new equity concerns because introverted or struggling students sometimes became less visible to the teacher. The authors conclude that LLM scaffolding in real-time K-12 classrooms needs to be proficiency-aware, cross-lingually informed, and better integrated with teacher oversight and classroom orchestration.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-family large language model chatbot used for interactive text generation, explanation, and feedback in writing tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Deployed as the underlying LLM in WriteAid to provide step-by-step writing support, sentence construction, grammar revision, and vocabulary/grammar explanations in real-time K-12 EFL classrooms.

findings.finding_summary: In a six-week deployment with 133 consenting eighth-grade students (157 total in the classes), LLM-supported sentence construction improved grammatical accuracy during in-class writing. Of 632 sentences constructed with the LLM in the fall semester, 309 (48.9%) were incorporated verbatim into students' final essays, and 82.3% of those incorporated sentences were grammatically correct.
findings.measure: Grammatical correctness of LLM-constructed sentences and whether those sentences were transferred into final essays

findings.finding_summary: Effects differed by performance group. High-performing students correctly incorporated 65.8% of LLM-constructed sentences into their final written assessments, whereas middle- and low-performing students did so only 37.8% and 14.0% of the time, respectively. The paper reports that lower-proficiency students were more likely to become demotivated and dependent on the system under step-by-step scaffolding.
findings.measure: Rate of correct incorporation of LLM-constructed sentences into final written assessment, by performance group

findings.finding_summary: Qualitative analysis found that lower-proficiency students often became overwhelmed, annoyed, or confused by step-by-step LLM feedback, especially later in the interaction. The paper reports that negative affective behaviors occurred on average 12.2 times per session for the middle-performing group and 11.4 times for the low-performing group, compared with 3.8 times for the high-performing group.
findings.measure: Affective responses during interaction (gratitude, annoyance, confusion, indifference)

findings.finding_summary: The LLM reduced teacher workload by handling simple questions and allowing the teacher to spend more time circulating in class. In the follow-up interview, the teacher reported having more time to walk around the classroom and check student progress because they no longer needed to answer every simple question.
findings.measure: Teacher workload and time available for classroom circulation, based on observation and interview

findings.finding_summary: The system had mixed effects on classroom equity. It helped more students complete tasks and may have narrowed completion gaps, but it also reduced questions from introverted students and made it harder for the teacher to identify common student difficulties because questions were split between the teacher and the AI.
findings.measure: Observed classroom participation, task completion, and teacher awareness of common difficulties

quality_tier_rationale: This is a single-site, mixed-methods classroom deployment study rather than an experimental efficacy trial. The paper provides rich qualitative and descriptive quantitative evidence, but it does not report causal effect sizes or randomized comparison conditions.
impact_tier_rationale: The study reports meaningful classroom benefits and harms, but the paper does not provide standardized effect sizes. Overall impact appears important operationally and pedagogically, but the magnitude is unclear from the reported data.
